name: Strike back when hit
summary: Every attack that lands on the unit from close by sets off an automatic strike back at the attacker: a bolt, a spike or a slice of the damage returned. Nothing is aimed, so even an unarmed unit punishes anyone who brawls with it, while attackers outside the radius take nothing back. Versions return a fixed amount or a share of the damage taken, answer only melee or anything within a short radius, hit just the attacker or everyone around, protect nearby allies as an aura, or come as a short window on a key that reflects shots. Raising a shield that only soaks damage is raise-shield; this one hurts the attacker. The levers are the radius, how much comes back, which attacks count and how often it can fire.
counterplay: Stay outside the radius: Arcing reaches only about two thirds of a rifle's range and Thorns Aura answers only melee, so ranged attackers hit it for free.
Bring tough attackers, or hit with fewer, bigger blows where the return is a fixed amount per attack: Warcraft III's bulky melee units barely feel Thorns Aura.
Soak the return: shields and damage reduction blunt it, as the Brawl Stars wiki warns for Jacky's Counter Crush against shielded tanks.
Switch it off where the game allows it: Dota's Break disables Centaur's Retaliate and Axe's Counter Helix.
Wait out an active window: reflect windows (Nyx Assassin's carapace, Genji's Deflect) last a moment and then wait out a cooldown, so hold fire until they drop.

other_examples.note: A passive aura that gives the hero and friendly units near him a damage shield: enemy melee attackers take back a share of the damage they deal, counted before armour. It does nothing against ranged attackers, and the wiki notes that players soon drop melee units or send bulky ones that barely feel it.

sources.title: Keeper of the Grove (Warcraft III), Warcraft Wiki

other_examples.unit: Spiked Carapace (Crypt Lord, The Frozen Throne)
other_examples.note: A passive that adds armour and sends a share of the damage from melee attackers back at them, so the Crypt Lord can wade into a fight and soak hits.

sources.title: Warcraft III: The Frozen Throne game manual (transcript), Warcraft Wiki
sources.note: Copies the game manual's hero entries, including the Crypt Lord's abilities.

other_examples.note: A passive that strikes back at every attack that lands on him, from any distance: a fixed amount plus a share of his strength, half as much against towers. Misses and spells don't set it off, Break disables it, and a talent spreads it to nearby allied heroes as an aura.

other_examples.unit: Counter Helix (Axe) and Spiked Carapace (Nyx Assassin)
other_examples.note: Axe's passive answers every set number of attacks on him with a spin that hits all enemies close to him; Break disables it. Nyx Assassin's Spiked Carapace is the form on a key: for a short time each attacker's damage is negated and sent back to them, once per attacker, and they are stunned.

An armour item whose passive deals magic damage back to anyone who hits the wearer with a basic attack and makes champions heal less for a short time. It fires even when a shield soaks the hit, but a dodge, a block or a miss stops it. The wiki suggests it against fast basic attackers and against those who heal through their attacks.

shooter_analogues.note: Whenever she takes damage she automatically smashes the ground around her, hitting every enemy within a short radius for about a third of the damage she took, without spending ammo. Two Jackys can't set each other off in a loop. The wiki's tips call it weak against long-range brawlers and strong against short-range assassins, and warn that shields blunt it.

A Paladin aura: monsters or players who hit him, or an ally inside the aura, with a melee attack take damage back, a fixed amount plus a multiple of the damage they dealt. It does nothing when they fail to land a hit, the returned damage can be resisted, and other players take only an eighth of it.

A shield on his back that stops one backstab: the Spy who tries it is locked out of attacking, cloaking and changing weapons for a couple of seconds, and a loud electric crack warns the Sniper, who can turn and fight. It breaks on use and grows back after a while, and a Sniper wearing it can't be overhealed.

On a short cooldown he raises his blade for up to about a second and a half: projectiles striking his front are sent back where he aims and melee attacks are blocked, while beams, area attacks and the heaviest projectiles get through. Reflected shots become his, so a reflected rocket can also splash him.

For an energy cost she wraps herself in a barrier for a while that cuts the damage of incoming gunfire and sends hitscan bullets straight back at the shooter at any range, while slower projectiles are deflected at random or toward a nearby enemy. It does nothing against area damage or melee.

player_translation.summary: A triggered defence that makes the unit dangerous to brawl with: any enemy that attacks it from inside a short radius is struck back at once, so flankers, melee units and close-range guns pay for every hit, while snipers and artillery are untouched. It suits slow, big or unarmed units that would otherwise be free prey for anyone who walks up to them.
as_user: You don't aim it: every attacker inside your ring is zapped as they hit you, so walking into a group of close-range enemies is a threat, not a death sentence.
You choose where to stand: hug enemies, sit in doorways and chokepoints, or hover over their short-range units so they must either shoot you and take the zap or stop shooting.
Against long-range enemies it does nothing, so you close the distance or get out of their sightlines.
On an unarmed unit it is your only damage, as Arcing is the Thunderhead's only way to harm anything: you score by being attacked.
as_target: A ring on the ground shows the strike-back radius; inside it, every shot you land on the unit sends a bolt back to you, with a crackle and a flash on your own health bar.
Step back out of the ring and keep shooting, switch to a long-range weapon, or leave it to your team's snipers and artillery.
If you must fight inside the ring, use few heavy hits or a shield; a fixed return per hit punishes rapid fire.
teammates: Its team uses it as a bodyguard against dives: melee units and flankers who chase a teammate into its ring pay for it, and the aura variant extends the protection to allies nearby.
Teammates with long range cover the gap it leaves against snipers and artillery.
The enemy team answers with long-range picks and keeps its brawlers away from it, so it shapes their unit choices.
controls: None: the base pattern is triggered by hits and spends no counted key.
The reflect-window variant puts a short reflect on Q, one counted key; the aura variant spends no key either.
feedback: A faint ring on the ground showing the radius, brightening for an enemy who steps inside.
Each strike back draws a bolt from the unit to the attacker with a crackle, so both sides see who was punished and why.
The attacker's health bar shows the returned damage in its own colour, with a small icon that names the cause.
For the reflect window, a bright shell and a distinct sound while it lasts, then a cooldown icon over the unit.
changes_from_rts: Tempest Rising's makers cut Arcing's damage and reach hard during the Veti multiplayer test, after players found Arcing units destroying armies by themselves; for players it stays support damage that punishes, not a weapon that wins fights alone.
RTS attackers keep auto-attacking whatever is nearest; players see the ring and can choose not to stand in it, so the radius must be readable and the return clear enough to learn from.
A per-hit trigger meets rapid-fire guns in a shooter: cap how often it fires at each attacker (one strike per short interval) so a machine gun doesn't draw a bolt for every bullet (proposal).
Stop loops: two strike-back units must not set each other off forever, which Brawl Stars fixed for two Jackys.
Area damage and damage over time need a rule: only direct hits from inside the ring set it off, so a grenade lobbed from outside draws no bolt (proposal).

team_play.notes: It shapes enemy picks: close-range and melee units suffer, long-range units ignore it. As an aura it protects nearby teammates from divers, and on a big unarmed unit it turns that unit into an obstacle that brawlers must respect.

notes: An on-damage hook that checks the attacker's distance and deals a set or proportional amount back.
Rules needed: a rate cap per attacker for rapid fire, which hits count (direct ones only), no loops between two such units, and what friendly fire and damage over time do.
Readable feedback (the ring and the bolt) is most of the work.
It grows with the number of attackers: against swarms of small units it can wipe out whole groups, which is why Tempest Rising's makers cut Arcing's damage and range so it would only support.
A return based on a share of the damage taken can kill an attacker who out-damages the unit, especially with armour on top; prefer a fixed amount with a rate cap.
An unarmed unit can still farm kills by parking over enemy brawlers; low damage keeps it a deterrent.
Returned damage is invisible unless the bolt is drawn, and players who die to it without seeing why feel cheated.
A ring on the ground clutters a busy top-down screen; show it faintly and brighten it only for enemies inside.

variants.name: Bolt back
variants.summary: Each attack from within a short radius draws one bolt of fixed damage back at the attacker; in some versions the bolt ignores armour.

variants.name: Melee thorns
variants.summary: Only melee attackers are hurt, taking back a share of the damage they deal; it often comes with extra armour.
variants.seen_in: Warcraft III Crypt Lord (Spiked Carapace), Diablo II Thorns

counters.why: Melee attackers take back a share of every blow they land on it.

variants.name: Thorns aura
variants.summary: Nearby allies get the same strike back against melee attackers, so the whole group is costly to brawl with.
variants.seen_in: Warcraft III Keeper of the Grove (Thorns Aura), Diablo II Paladin (Thorns), Dota 2 Centaur Warrunner (Retaliate with its talent)

variants.name: Counter shockwave
variants.summary: A hit taken, or every few hits, sets off a burst around the unit that hurts every enemy nearby, not only the attacker.
variants.seen_in: Brawl Stars Jacky (Counter Crush), Dota 2 Axe (Counter Helix)

variants.name: Anti-heal thorns
variants.summary: Basic attacks on the unit cost the attacker health and cut the healing they receive for a moment.

variants.name: Charge the attacker
variants.summary: The strike back also puts a slowing status on vehicles it hurts.
variants.seen_in: Tempest Rising Lifeblood Curse doctrine (Arcing adds Tempest Charge)

variants.name: Reflect window
variants.summary: On a key, for a moment, attacks on the unit are turned back: shots fly back toward the attacker or where the unit aims, and in some versions attackers are stunned; then a cooldown.
variants.seen_in: Dota 2 Nyx Assassin (Spiked Carapace), Overwatch Genji (Deflect), Warframe Mesa (Shatter Shield)

adds_weaknesses.why: The reflection lasts only a moment and then waits out a cooldown, so attackers hold fire until it drops.

variants.name: Shock the ambusher
variants.summary: A one-off charge on the unit's back stops the first ambush from behind and locks the attacker out of attacking for a moment, without hurting it, then grows back after a while.

adds_strengths.why: Every enemy that attacks it from close range is struck back automatically, so brawlers and flankers pay for each hit.

adds_weaknesses.why: The strike back reaches only nearby attackers; anything firing from outside its radius hits it freely.

counters.why: Melee and short-range attackers have to stand inside the strike-back radius, so every hit they land costs them health.

countered_by.why: Long-range attackers stay outside the radius and take nothing back.
Tough attackers shrug off the small return damage, as bulky melee units do against Warcraft III's Thorns Aura.

open_questions: Pattern or armour model? The fit notes asked for a pattern because no armour model covers damage returned to an attacker, and the Tempest Rising registry note records Arcing as a triggered ability; a word-list term would suit if many cards should carry it as plain protection.
Fixed damage per hit or a share of the damage taken? (Recommended: fixed, with a rate cap per attacker, so rapid fire and swarms don't explode.)
Should it ever answer attackers outside the radius, as Dota's Retaliate answers attacks from any distance?
May a card carry it as its only damage, as the unarmed Thunderhead does?

shooter_fit.reason: Proven in a top-down shooter (Brawl Stars' Counter Crush) and readable as a ring plus a bolt; it gives slow, big or unarmed units a reason for brawlers to keep away, but it needs a rate cap against rapid-fire guns.
